expectations.text: Keeps the drafted constraints to things a judge could actually check
expectations.evidence: The draft has five constraints, and most are concrete enough to verify in a demo: 'must not require new in-store hardware', 'output must reach an associate in one action, not a dashboard', 'must not use real customer or employee personal data', and 'must work from data a store already has: [POS sales, stock counts, planogram]'. The response makes checkability an explicit design rule twice: 'Write them so a judge can verify each one by looking at the demo' and 'Every constraint is checkable by a judge.' It also uses the ISRO '<100 ms' example to show a constraint can carry a number. Points are

expectations.text: Keeps the drafted constraints to things a judge could actually check
expectations.evidence: Most floor constraints can be checked: `make run` must write `out/alerts.jsonl` with named fields and a 0–1 confidence; the held-out precision/recall metric is defined (top 20 alerts per store per shift, at least 2 h of lead time); the 10-submission cap and every-2-hours limit are concrete; and the floor test checks schema and runtime. Several constraints are weaker. Constraint 4, 'never uses data timestamped after the alert's ts', is very hard to verify, and `test_no_lookahead` is left as `...` with only a vague comment about 'logged data access', so no check is designed.
